claims.text: In tungsten-based alloys at 1300–1500 °C, high-temperature plastic strain and toughness are governed by the fraction of engineered coherent twin boundaries and low-Σ CSL boundaries.
Coherent twin boundaries and low-Σ CSL boundaries are effective barriers to dislocation pile-up.
These engineered boundaries delay the onset of localized plastic flow.
Delaying localized plastic flow through twin-boundary engineering enhances toughness.
The conventional tungsten-based baseline has a random grain-boundary distribution.
Controlled annealing combined with mechanical pre-straining can maximize coherent twin-boundary and low-Σ CSL-boundary fractions in a tungsten-based alloy.
Engineered coherent twin boundaries physically obstruct dislocations.
Engineered coherent twin boundaries distribute dislocations more uniformly.
Twin boundaries and low-energy CSL interfaces obstruct dislocation motion.
Preventing dislocation pile-up reduces local stress concentrations.
Reduced local stress concentrations delay catastrophic plastic flow and produce more uniform plastic deformation.
More uniform plastic deformation preserves toughness at high temperatures.
Relative to conventionally processed tungsten, the boundary-engineered alloy will have lower localized plastic strain and reduced creep rates.
Relative to conventionally processed tungsten, the boundary-engineered alloy will have greater energy to fracture and improved toughness.
Degradation of engineered twin boundaries into high-angle or incoherent boundaries will result in performance similar to or worse than the baseline.
The proposed mechanism should hold in tungsten-based alloys between 1300 and 1500 °C under plasma-facing-component loading conditions.
Prolonged exposure, microstructural coarsening, or loss of twin-boundary integrity may limit the mechanism.

contradictions.description: Loss or degradation of the engineered boundaries is presented as a boundary condition that removes the proposed cause and is predicted to eliminate the benefit, but the falsification rule also treats boundary degradation itself as falsification. Degradation would show failure to maintain the intervention rather than necessarily falsifying the mechanism when intact boundaries are present.

The experiment imposes a constant strain rate while also treating a reduced creep rate as a comparative outcome. An imposed strain rate cannot itself be lower in one specimen group; a separate constant-stress creep protocol or a clearly defined local creep-rate measurement is needed.
